newsitem.title: USA: Cocoa prices rise, coffee and oil fall back.
newsitem.headline: Cocoa prices rise, coffee and oil fall back.

text.p: Cocoa prices rose on Friday in a rebound from recent heavy selling, while both coffee and oil prices closed lower on profit-taking.
At New York's Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange, March cocoa jumped $48 per metric ton to close at $1,308 as traders bought back into the market after selling heavily earlier this week.
"It started the day oversold technically," said Smith Barney analyst Walter Spilka. "It was inevitably going to go up at some point."
Despite the market's recent wild ride, the fundamental outlook for cocoa was little changed.

While early estimates for the 1996/97 crop in the Ivory Coast, the world's biggest producer, had called for a yield well below last year's record total, Spilka said the market's recent slump to 10-month lows indicated stockpiles were probably in good shape.
"The way the market acts, there is more cocoa out there than the numbers are showing," Spilka said. "The crop probably isn't going to come in a whole lot smaller than last year."
Coffee, which has grabbed the spotlight by rising more than 30 percent since Dec. 6, fell as traders took profits.
March coffee closed down 3.15 cents a pound at 136.90 cents, but not before setting a new contract high at 142.60 cents. That price was the highest since September 1995.
The March contract overall gained 12.90 cents -- or more than 10 percent -- this week on worries about coffee supply.

A nine-day dockworkers' strike at Colombia's Buenaventura port was settled late Thursday, which would free up shipments of some 300,000 bags of coffee exports blocked by the strike. Each bag weighs 132 pounds.
"Because of the resolution of the Colombian strike, the market corrected," said Refco Inc. analyst Ann Prendergast.
Traders also cited recent estimates that the 1997/98 coffee crop in top producer Brazil could be down 20 percent or more from last season's 25 million bags.
A producer group, the Association of Coffee Producing Countries, agreed Thursday to cut their coffee exports by 1.3 million bags between January and June 1997 to keep prices from falling.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, gasoline prices fell following restart of a key refinery unit and news of gasoline imports headed for New York Harbor, traders said.
February gasoline ended 0.67 cent a gallon lower at 67.75 cents, and March crude oil fell 13 cents to $24.05 a barrel.
Tosco Corp. restarted a 140,000 barrel-per-day catalytic cracker, used to make gasoline, at its Bayway refinery in Linden, N.J., this week. Traders also cited deals for gasoline cargoes from Europe.

"Gasoline had firmed when Tosco was having problems, so now that it has restarted, the feeling is we certainly won't need these cargoes coming over," said Nauman Barakat, a trader with Prudential Securities in New York.

February heating oil bucked the selling in other markets to close 0.42 cent a gallon higher at 66.77 cents. Another bout with winter weather was expected in the Midwest over the weekend, increasing heating fuel demand.
New York precious metals futures ended higher again led by silver as the recent strong rallies in the dollar and stock market staged a correction for the second day in a row.
March silver ended up 10.2 cents at $4.977 an ounce on the New York Mercantile Exchange's Comex division after posting a session high of $5, the highest level for the contract since late November.
February gold ended up 90 cents at $353.40 an ounce.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, March soybeans closed up 6-1/4 cents at $7.47-1/2 a bushel, and March corn up 2-1/2 cents at $2.72-3/4 as strong export sales bolstered sentiment.

The Agriculture Department said net exports of soybeans during the week ended Jan. 16 totaled 447,000 metric tons, above expectations for 300,000 to 400,000 tons. Sales of corn were 1.262 million tons, well above analyst guesses of 500,000 to 800,000 tons.
